title: Domestication of the chicken
summary: Chickens descend mainly from the red junglefowl subspecies Gallus gallus spadiceus of south-western China, Thailand and Myanmar. A genetic split is estimated at about 9,500 years ago, but the first unambiguous domestic chicken bones come from Neolithic Ban Non Wat in Thailand, about 1650 to 1250 BCE. Their appearance with rice and millet farming suggests stored grain drew junglefowl into human settlements. Chickens reached China, South Asia and Mesopotamia in the late second millennium BCE and Mediterranean Europe by about 800 BCE; they are now the most numerous domestic animal.

uncertainty.note: Peters et al. 2022: first unambiguous domestic chickens at Ban Non Wat, c. 1650-1250 BCE; in Ethiopia and Mediterranean Europe by c. 800 BCE. Wang et al. 2020 estimate a genetic split from G. g. spadiceus about 9500 +/- 3300 years ago, which need not mark domestication.

importance.justification: Produced the most numerous domestic animal, a staple food across the world (R4 D2 T4 L2).

beats.caption: Wild red junglefowl were attracted to early rice cultivation at sites like Ban Non Wat, establishing domestic lineages.
Domestic chickens spread across Asia, Africa, and the Mediterranean, becoming the world's most widespread domestic bird.
